source_document.body:
Editor’s note: Rob Carpenter is an independent contributor to FreightWaves. The reporting, analysis and opinions in this piece are his own and do not necessarily reflect the views of FreightWaves or its affiliates.
On July 2, 2026, a Michigan inspector pulled over a truck running under USDOT 2566250, registered to Gamboa Logistic Inc. of Beavercreek, Ohio, and by the time the stop was finished the driver had collected 11 hours-of-service violations, seven of them for tampering with the electronic logging device that exists for the single purpose of making sure a driver, a dispatcher and an inspector are all looking at the same clock. The other four were for driving past the 11-hour and 14-hour limits. Each tampering count was an out-of-service violation, meaning the truck did not move again until the driver was back in compliance.
A year earlier, on July 4, 2025, the same company filed four applications with the Labor Department to bring in 30 heavy truck drivers under the H-2B temporary worker program, at $29.78 to $31.38 an hour, for that Beavercreek worksite. The department denied all four that August. In 24 months of federal inspection data, Gamboa’s trucks ran up 13 English proficiency violations, seven of them out of service, eight drivers with no valid CDL, four driving on a suspended or disqualified CDL, a fatigue out-of-service, and a drug out-of-service. Its trucks were also involved in two crashes that killed three people, and FMCSA crash records show involvement, not fault.
The electronic logging device exists so a driver, a dispatcher and an inspector all read the same clock. The visa system exists so a company that needs workers must prove it cannot find them here and must pay a fair wage to bring them in. The Training Provider Registry exists so the person behind the wheel actually learned to drive the truck. The SBA’s pandemic programs existed to keep real businesses alive. Every one of those systems runs on the same assumption, that the company filing the paperwork is the company doing the work. This series has already followed one owner, Dragos Sprinceana, from a Gold Coast fleet FMCSA shut down in 2023 with $889,630 in penalties to a vice president’s seat at a Miami immigration nonprofit this spring, and asked who decides who sits in the seat. This piece goes looking for the seats, and at the contradiction running underneath the crackdown, that the same federal government now pulling foreign drivers out of American trucks keeps clearing and certifying the carriers that put them there, in one case a carrier FMCSA itself had already shut down.
554 Carriers, One Screen
The Labor Department publishes every employer request it decides under the PERM program, the first step in an employment-based green card, and under the H-2A and H-2B temporary worker programs, each filing naming the employer, its phone and address, the job, the wage and the outcome. I pulled every PERM filing for fiscal 2024 through 2026 and every H-2A and H-2B filing for fiscal 2024 through 2027, kept the ones for truck drivers, and matched the employers to FMCSA’s carrier census on strong signals only, the same phone and name, or the same phone in the same state. The screen returned 554 motor carriers that asked to sponsor foreign truck drivers.
Then I compared them with everyone else. Among active carriers with 10 or more trucks that FMCSA’s Safety Measurement System scores, 31.1% are in alert in at least one safety category, 17,344 of 55,823. Among PERM truck-driver sponsors of the same size, the rate is 50.4%, 57 of 113. Among H-2B truck-driver sponsors it is 48.3%. Farms that sponsor H-2A drivers to haul their own crops run at 24.3%, below the industry average. The widest gap is hours of service : 35.4% of the PERM sponsors FMCSA measures in that category are in alert, against 21.2% for all carriers with 10 or more trucks. Driver Fitness, the category that catches drivers without valid licenses or medical cards, runs 15.6% for sponsors against 8.8% for the industry.
Here is the fair concession, and it matters. A PERM filing is a request. It does not mean a worker ever entered the country, and a sponsored driver may be completely lawful. Most PERM driver petitions are for people already here who become permanent residents and get an ordinary CDL, and the non-domiciled CDL rule does not touch that path and was never meant to. Inspection records do not say which driver was sponsored, so this data does not show that a sponsored driver caused any violation. The defensible sentence is narrow: carriers that ask to sponsor foreign drivers carry these safety records. Plenty of sponsors are clean, and some of the most respected names in trucking file PERM petitions every year because they cannot fill seats.
The concentration is not random. Illinois, mostly the Chicago suburbs, accounts for 83 of 242 PERM sponsor carriers and 504 of 1,968 PERM filings. Florida’s sponsor list is mostly farms. Ohio has only five PERM sponsor carriers. The Chicago book is the same ground this series has walked from the start: Elgin, Wheeling, Mount Prospect, Elk Grove Village, Alsip, Lisle. The problem starts at the margins.
What The Rules Say Now
Three federal changes since 2025 set the stage. On June 25, 2025, the Commercial Vehicle Safety Alliance put English language proficiency back into the North American Out-of-Service Criteria under 49 CFR 391.11(b)(2), after the April 28, 2025, executive order, so a driver who cannot communicate with an officer is now parked, not just written up. On Feb. 13, 2026, FMCSA published its final rule on non-domiciled CDLs, 91 Fed. Reg. 7044, effective March 16, limiting those licenses to drivers in H-2A, H-2B or E-2 status, ending the use of work permits as proof, and capping the license at the worker’s authorized stay or one year. The D.C. Circuit denied emergency stays on May 5, so the rule is in force while the challenge proceeds. Read that rule next to the Labor Department data and H-2B becomes one of three remaining doors to a non-domiciled CDL, and the H-2B sponsor list is where some of this story’s worst records sit. On Dec. 1, 2025, FMCSA said it would stop letting ELD registrations flow straight from a vendor’s self-certification onto its public list and would cross-check new applications against revoked devices, acknowledging in its own words that the old system made it easier to re-register revoked devices. That is the agency describing the hole after it had been open for eight years.
Gamboa, An Aged Number And A Hypergrowth Fleet
USDOT 2566250 was added to FMCSA’s census on Dec. 18, 2014. Its only crash before 2024 lists a Miami Beach address, in 2015. Then the number goes quiet for roughly nine years, until Gamboa Logistic Inc. filed new articles of incorporation in Ohio on Oct. 4, 2023, with Mustafa Emir Yildirim as incorporator and statutory agent, and the first inspection under the revived number came in February 2024. An old DOT number matters because brokers, shippers and insurers read age as stability. A number added in 2014 clears filters a 2024 number does not. The record on file is a decade old. The company behind it is three years old.
The phone on Gamboa’s FMCSA record is a New York City number, its trucks run New York apportioned plates, and Yildirim’s other companies list a Brooklyn address, while the Ohio address carries a suite number that reads like a mailbox. On its Oct. 29, 2026, MCS-150, Gamboa told FMCSA it runs 683 power units and 683 drivers and drove more than 64 million miles. In the inspection data, 212 distinct power-unit VINs have run under the number, and those 212 tractors have also been inspected under 136 other carriers’ numbers, with 62 pieces of equipment that first ran for carriers now dead resurfacing under Gamboa. Equipment sharing is a lead, not a verdict, because trucks get sold, leased and repossessed every day. But a fleet that declares 683 trucks while showing 212 at the roadside, pulled from a pool that touches 136 other carriers, is not the single, self-contained fleet a shipper might picture, and the inspection record fairly raises the question of how much of what runs under the number Gamboa itself controls.
In the same 24 months, Gamboa logged 604 inspections, 831 violations and 25 crashes, and sits in alert in five SMS categories, with Crash Indicator, Unsafe Driving and Driver Fitness all at the 96th percentile. Its vehicle out-of-service rate is 29.2% against a 23.2% national average, and it has never been given a safety rating, even though by its own filing it puts 683 trucks on the road. The tampering is not a one-off: 11 ELD tampering counts in two years, every one out of service, including the seven-count Michigan stop, two counts in Oregon in April, tampering plus two false logs in Ohio in September, and a suspended-CDL-plus-tampering stop in Iowa on Oct. 20, three weeks before this piece was written. A crash suit, Freeland v. Gamboa Logistic Inc., W.D. La. No. 2:25-cv-01523, is pending, and whoever defends it will eventually have to produce the ELD edit history the Michigan inspector was looking at.
Polmax, The Whole Pipeline In One Building
If Gamboa is what the data looks like from the outside, Polmax is what the court record looks like from the inside. Polmax LLC, USDOT 758399, doing business as Experior Transport, operates from 12161 S. Central Ave. in Alsip, Illinois, holds a Satisfactory rating, runs 106 trucks, and is not a fly-by-night operation. It is also the largest truck-driver PERM filer in the Chicago book, 133 filings in fiscal 2025 and 2026, more than its truck count.
Follow a driver through it. Illinois job postings for Experior Transport ask for an Illinois CDL or one within 60 days of employment, the language that shows up in PERM recruitment ads. The training is in-house, with Experior Truck Driving School listed on FMCSA’s Training Provider Registry at the same 12161 S. Central Ave. address. The driver is then signed as a contractor. In Komorski v. Polmax Logistics LLC, Cook County Chancery No. 2021-CH-01601, drivers alleged they were misclassified as independent contractors, charged unlawful deductions and denied final pay, and Polmax agreed to a $1.5 million class settlement while admitting no wrongdoing. It was not the first wage case, Kawa v. Polmax LLC in 2013 named Tomasz Dulian, and Galeano v. Polmax LLC, filed in February 2025, is still open and names Dulian and Zbigniew Loszewski individually.
The ELD answer is in the Komorski file. The independent-contractor agreement filed there names Samsara Networks Inc. as the vendor for both the ELD and the event recorder, a mainstream, fully registered device. So when FMCSA data shows Polmax drivers with 16 false-log violations and 27 over-hours violations in 24 months, including eight false-log counts in one New York stop, the problem is not a rogue logbook company. The device records, and who altered any individual log the public data cannot say, which is exactly why anyone litigating against Polmax should ask Samsara for the edit history it keeps. Its HOS percentile is 90, in alert, and its trucks were cited for parking unlawfully on the roadway three times between early September and mid-October 2026. A truck on a shoulder often means a driver out of hours with nowhere to stop, which is an indicator, not proof.
Then the structure and the money. Illinois filings list Lynx Management Inc., president Tomasz Dulian, as manager of a string of Polmax entities, and a separate fleet LLC is ordinary in trucking, except it also lets the trucks sit under a different company from the one carrying the operating authority and the crash exposure. SBA disclosure data shows Polmax LLC took two Paycheck Protection Program loans totaling about $1.85 million, all forgiven, and two smaller Polmax names in the same building drew PPP money too, neither with active for-hire authority and neither inspected in 24 months. What sits in that one Alsip building is nearly every function a driver passes through: recruitment, a training school, the contractor agreement, the ELD, a separate fleet LLC holding the trucks, and the entities that drew the federal payroll money. Each of those is lawful on its own, Polmax holds a Satisfactory safety rating and admitted no wrongdoing in Komorski, and the point is not that any single piece is improper. The point is how much of a driver’s working life can run through companies tied to one address, and what that concentration means for the driver in the middle.
Certified While Shut Down
Gold Coast’s operating company, DMG Consulting, filed an H-1B labor condition application in April 2024, seven months after FMCSA put it out of service, and the Labor Department certified it in a week. That was not a one-off. MFUPRZ LLC, USDOT 2960394, has been under a federal out-of-service order since Sept. 7, 2021, with its for-hire authority revoked and a Conditional safety rating, and its last MCS-150 was filed in April 2021. On Oct. 16, 2024, three years into that shutdown order, the Labor Department certified MFUPRZ to bring in 39 H-2B truck drivers for a Dallas worksite, along with dozens of truck-driver helpers and material handlers across two states. Under the rule that took effect in March, H-2B is one of the three statuses that still qualify for a non-domiciled CDL.
An H-2B certification is a labor certification, not a CDL, and the public data does not show whether visas issued or who drove. MFUPRZ may run a warehouse or contract its drivers to another carrier, which would be legal. But the Labor Department has no field in its process that asks whether the employer is a motor carrier under a federal shutdown order, and no one at FMCSA reads Labor Department certifications. Mercator Global Logistics LLC of Elk Grove Village makes the same point in miniature: it filed 48 PERM truck-driver petitions in December 2023 while its FMCSA record showed one truck, one driver, three involuntary revocations and an inactive status. Forty-eight drivers for one truck.
The Rest Of The Chicago Book
The other names follow a pattern you can read in the inspection data. Planet Logistics, 91 trucks and 55 PERM filings, sits in alert on Vehicle Maintenance with a 34.5% vehicle out-of-service rate and 22 tire out-of-service violations. Grasshopper Trans, 30 trucks and 28 PERM filings, sits in alert on hours of service, and its 2023 MCS-150 claims about 232,682 miles per truck, when a hard-running team truck does 200,000. Profit Logistic, doing business as MP Freight, posts a 43.8% vehicle out-of-service rate. And Go To Logistics, 44 trucks and 27 PERM filings, holds a Satisfactory rating with no category in alert, and the six deaths on its record are all the Feb. 11, 2021, I-35W pileup in Fort Worth, where FMCSA credits all six deaths to every carrier with a truck in the chain. Go To had one truck in it. It belongs on the sponsor list and does not belong in the bad-carrier paragraph.
One fact cuts against the easy story. All of these carriers have a driver out-of-service rate below the 6.4% national average, Gamboa’s is 5.8% and Polmax’s is 2.4%, so as inspected, the drivers are mostly qualified on paper. The two things the company controls are hours and equipment, and those run hot. Across all 11 USDOT numbers in the sponsor workbook, FMCSA’s crash file holds 318 crashes, 13 deaths and 225 injuries, and taking out the Fort Worth pileup leaves 317 crashes, seven deaths and 139 injuries. Crash records show involvement, not fault.
The Logbook Layer
Every one of those hours violations ran through a device on FMCSA’s registered list, and that list has a structural problem that predates any of these carriers. An analysis of the registry found 178 registered devices held by 172 nominally separate companies across 28 states, all sharing a single sequential identifier counter running from 101 to 279, with the first character swapped to match the brand name in 177 of 178 cases, and the companies sharing no phones, no websites and no addresses. White labeling is legal and common, and names like TrackEnsure and ONE20 on that list have nothing to do with any of this. But 35 more registrations run on one platform identifier, PT30, under 35 company names in 20 states, almost all registered to free Gmail accounts, and when FMCSA revoked Green Light ELD in November 2025 the notice listed the model as “PT30, IOSiX.” The giveaway in the field is a driver’s record that follows the device rather than the truck, the same named driver turning up on two unrelated companies’ ELDs in different states, because the driver record lives in a shared database under the brand.
The rule that is supposed to prevent exactly this is 49 CFR 395.30 and Appendix A to its subpart, which require that any edited log entry carry an unchangeable event-status code, origin code and timestamp, precisely so a driver, an officer or a plaintiff’s lawyer can tell a legitimate correction from a cover-up. The Cook County case that put names on the problem is Owirodu v. Extra Mile International Inc., No. 2024CH06818, a class action over logbook manipulation sold to Chicago-area carriers. In a motion there, the plaintiffs’ lawyers describe two groups, a Murzac enterprise built around Phoenix ELD LLC, and a Colibri enterprise they call the “Bolt ELD LLC/Colibri ELD LLC web,” and allege both kept overwriting and deleting drivers’ hours-of-service records after a May 2025 protective order. Those are allegations in a pending case, and no one has been found liable. The motion describes a Matryoshka structure in which a registered provider swore it did not own the software platform or have access to its source code, and points upstream to a platform whose website, in the motion’s description, invited customers to “cook up” their logs. On Jan. 6, 2026, a judge authorized subpoenas to banks, payment processors and the individuals involved. One thread runs through Gold Coast itself, where records subpoenaed in that case show the federally registered Bolt ELD device carrying a support phone that rings on Gold Coast’s own RingCentral account.
The Form That Is Supposed To Make A Carrier Reachable
There is a second blind spot, and it decides what happens after a truck like Gamboa’s kills someone. Every carrier operating across state lines must file a BOC-3, naming a person or company in each state to accept a lawsuit on the carrier’s behalf. It is a one-page form that costs about $20, and its entire purpose is to make sure that when a truck kills somebody two states from where it is registered, the family’s lawyer has somewhere to send a process server. An analysis of the complete federal BOC-3 file, 1,690,743 rows covering 1,668,695 carriers, found 231,217 of them, nearly 14% of the entire federally authorized fleet, naming one of two companies operating out of a single suite in Sioux Falls, South Dakota. It found 336,458 carriers with the agent field left entirely blank, and 18,711 more who simply typed the word “Carrier” into a field FMCSA’s own instructions say only a process agent, broker or freight forwarder may fill. Ninety-two percent of Mexico-domiciled carriers in the file have no valid process-agent designation, and a spot check of 40 against FMCSA’s live authority system found 39 still cleared to run on American highways.
This is not a gap anyone has to discover. FMCSA wrote in a 2019 policy document that the designation must exist at all times for a carrier’s registration to stay valid, and that its own enforcement staff had reported being unable to complete service of process when a designation went stale. The agency put in writing seven years ago that the gate does not hold. Pair it with the equipment data and the picture is complete: the truck moves to a new DOT number within days of a revocation, and the paper trail that was supposed to make the operator reachable was never built to catch a move that fast.
The Wage Layer
The logbook and the paycheck are the same document seen from two sides. A driver paid by the mile, charged for his truck and told the violations will disappear has every reason to keep driving and no way to prove later how many hours he actually worked. Gold Coast showed what that looks like in a federal judgment: in Ealom v. Goldcoast Carriers Inc., N.D. Ill. No. 1:24-cv-05217, the court found the defendants, including Sprinceana personally, liable under the Fair Labor Standards Act and the Illinois Wage Payment and Collection Act, and Anthony Ealom’s July 2023 settlement statement shows net pay of negative $2,202.08 after a $2,500 “Equipment Recovery Fee.” He finished a week of work owing his carrier money.
Super Ego is the larger version. Atkinson v. Super Ego Holding LLC, N.D. Ill. No. 1:22-cv-04127, is a putative class action alleging misclassification and unlawful deductions across a network of carriers, and a review of the inspection data turns up six carriers downstream of the Super Ego and Mimic cluster, each declaring seven or eight trucks to FMCSA while running between 170 and 260 vehicles pulled from three predecessor carriers already in litigation, all added to the census in 2024 or 2025, each identifiable from the shared-equipment pattern alone. The human version is Svyatoslav Likanov, who came to the United States from St. Petersburg. He told our reporter Clarissa Hawes that he drove car carriers for Amstel Inc. up to 140 hours a week, that dispatchers falsified his electronic logs, and that a video urging Russians to come on tourist visas steered him into the job. We reported that Amstel drivers were cited 49 times for driving without a CDL before its authority was revoked, and that Likanov and his family went into hiding after he went public. Amstel’s owners did not respond to our requests for comment. The pattern he described, recruitment through community networks, pay held back, debt that grows with every deduction, and a log that says whatever dispatch needs, is the pattern the court files describe in legal language.
The School Layer
ELDT, the entry-level driver training rule, took effect in February 2022, set a federal floor for CDL training and a registry of approved schools, and let the schools certify themselves. On Dec. 1, 2025, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy announced FMCSA had removed nearly 3,000 providers from the Training Provider Registry and put thousands more on notice, out of 39,554 training locations then listed. Before those removals, a match of the registry against carrier crash and network records had flagged two schools that FMCSA itself later removed on March 20, 2026. The fair concession here is large: 60% of all school-to-carrier links in the registry are simply carriers training their own drivers, like Experior Truck Driving School training for Polmax, which is legal and often the best training in the industry. The risk is the vertical, when the same group recruits the driver, trains him, employs him and, in some states, tests him, because then the federal floor depends entirely on that company’s honesty.
The Money Layer
Earlier this year I matched the SBA’s EIDL and PPP files against FMCSA’s carrier census and found $7.99 billion in EIDL loans to 85,493 carriers, including 17,631 carriers that drew $1.46 billion in EIDL loans even though their USDOT numbers were created after the program’s eligibility date. Run the foreign-driver sponsor list through the same files and 110 sponsor carriers drew 137 PPP loans totaling $50.6 million, $46.0 million of it forgiven, with 42 drawing EIDL loans and five of those having USDOT numbers created after the cutoff. Most of that money went to real fleets with real 2020 payrolls. The point is not that sponsors took loans. The point is that the same federal paperwork, a DOT number, an MC number and an insurance filing, satisfied three agencies at once, and none of them looked at what the others held.
That gap has a sharper version in the insurance file. A cross-reference of the 348 carriers insured by Compass Specialty Insurance Risk Retention Group, a Tennessee-domiciled group writing trucking liability at the federal minimum, against the SBA’s EIDL file found 65 of those carriers holding EIDL loans, and 38 Compass carriers showing a policy issued and canceled the same day, with zero power units and zero inspections, 11 of which received EIDL loans. A carrier activates authority on an insurance certificate, the certificate expires the same day, and the credential package left in FMCSA’s file matches exactly what a trucking company needs for an EIDL application. Compass and its affiliates have been in federal court on this before, in a 2020 complaint and a 2021 False Claims Act case that alleged false insurance certificates were filed with FMCSA. The United States declined to intervene, and the court dismissed both cases without prejudice on procedural grounds, so neither was decided on the merits.
How It Works
Put the layers together and a single pattern recurs across the files, a composite assembled from many carriers’ records rather than a description of any one company named above. In the abstract, it has four parts. It starts with a DOT number, ideally an old one, inherited, bought with the company that holds it, or revived behind a number that went dormant years ago. It runs on a logbook that says what dispatch needs, whether from a white-label vendor that sells “monitoring” or from a mainstream device whose records someone in the office is willing to edit. It leans on drivers who cannot push back, sponsored, indebted, paid by the mile, signed as contractors, trained in a company school, and told the violation will disappear. And it keeps the assets at arm’s length, the trucks in a fleet LLC, the authority in an operating company, the payroll money in whichever entity qualifies, so that when a crash comes, the plaintiff finds a shell and a process agent who never answers.
The inspection data shows the moves at scale. Starting from 47 seed carriers across nine known networks, including Gold Coast and Pony Express, Commontrans, Denver Cargo, AAA Freight, the Super Ego and Mimic successors, and Compass and MGR, a review of every truck they ran turned up 1,657 carriers that shared at least one vehicle, and after setting aside big fleets, lessors, one-off sales and junk VINs, 101 met the threshold for direct equipment entanglement. Leader Freight Systems declares five trucks and has run 194, and 182 of them went on to Denver Cargo. A compliance firm’s mock DOT audit this fall of two separately filed carriers put the same mechanism under a hand check, finding identical ELD login credentials used across both driver rosters, tractors and trailers interchanged between the two fleets within the same week, and one safety manager listed as the point of contact for both. Two carriers that look like competitors in the federal registry were, in practice, one operation splitting its paper trail in two. None of the individual moves is necessarily illegal. A PERM petition is legal, a company school is legal, a contractor agreement is legal until a court says otherwise, a white-label ELD is legal, and a PPP loan was legal. No carrier named in this piece has been shown to run that full sequence, and several hold clean safety ratings. What none of the federal agencies does is look at all of it at once, and the risk lives in the space between them.
What Would Close It
None of this needs a new law. The Labor Department can check every employer certification filed by a motor carrier against FMCSA’s out-of-service list, matched on the employer’s federal ID number, before it certifies, and MFUPRZ and DMG would both have failed that check. FMCSA can require every ELD registration to name its owners and its upstream software licensor under penalty of perjury, and refuse registrations that share a platform identifier with a revoked device until the licensor answers. It can treat an ELD tampering out-of-service violation as an automatic trigger for an off-site investigation, and Gamboa has 11 of them and no safety rating. It can reject a BOC-3 that names no valid process agent, or names one its own records show is stale, and refuse to keep a registration active without a real one. The Training Provider Registry can flag every provider that shares an address, phone or officer with a motor carrier and require that carrier’s crash and hours record to come with the school’s self-certification. And the SBA’s Office of Inspector General already runs a hotline, with the referral package built.
Why It Matters
The federal crackdown is aimed at the seat, and the record is about the companies that sold the seat, logged the seat and borrowed against it. This series has already told the story of Rocky Chhean, who drove for Gold Coast until the night he died in one of its trucks, and whose name the company later typed onto its registered-agent form five years after he was buried. This one ends on the drivers whose names are not in any of these records. The inspection data does not list them, the visa data does not carry them, and the court files call them putative class members. One of them sat in a truck in Michigan on July 2 while an officer counted seven tampering violations on a device that was supposed to protect him. Every system in this story, the logbook, the visa, the training registry, the process agent, the pandemic loan, was built on the belief that the company filing the paperwork is the company doing the work. For a measurable, named slice of the industry, that belief is false, and no single agency is positioned to notice.

On Dec. 1, 2025, FMCSA said it would stop letting ELD registrations flow straight from a vendor’s self-certification onto its public list and would cross-check new applications against revoked devices, acknowledging in its own words that the old system made it easier to re-register revoked devices.

MFUPRZ LLC, USDOT 2960394, has been under a federal out-of-service order since Sept. 7, 2021, with its for-hire authority revoked and a Conditional safety rating, and its last MCS-150 was filed in April 2021.

On Oct. 16, 2024, three years into that shutdown order, the Labor Department certified MFUPRZ to bring in 39 H-2B truck drivers for a Dallas worksite, along with dozens of truck-driver helpers and material handlers across two states.
An H-2B certification is a labor certification, not a CDL, and the public data does not show whether visas issued or who drove.
But the Labor Department has no field in its process that asks whether the employer is a motor carrier under a federal shutdown order, and no one at FMCSA reads Labor Department certifications.

In a motion there, the plaintiffs’ lawyers describe two groups, a Murzac enterprise built around Phoenix ELD LLC, and a Colibri enterprise they call the “Bolt ELD LLC/Colibri ELD LLC web,” and allege both kept overwriting and deleting drivers’ hours-of-service records after a May 2025 protective order.

A cross-reference of the 348 carriers insured by Compass Specialty Insurance Risk Retention Group, a Tennessee-domiciled group writing trucking liability at the federal minimum, against the SBA’s EIDL file found 65 of those carriers holding EIDL loans, and 38 Compass carriers showing a policy issued and canceled the same day, with zero power units and zero inspections, 11 of which received EIDL loans.
